analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set safe registered-nurse staffing levels with frontline nurses deciding.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required Medicare hospitals to set safe registered-nurse staffing levels with 55 percent direct-care nurse committees, was introduced in June 2010 with no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that takes Medicare patients to write a hospital-wide staffing plan guaranteeing enough registered nurses on each unit and shift for safe care. Each hospital would have had to set up a staffing committee where at least 55 percent of members are direct-care registered nurses — not managers — and the plan would have had to include adjustable minimum nurse numbers, limits on unsafe assignments, and a nurse's right to refuse an assignment that violates the plan. Hospitals would have to post daily staffing numbers publicly, report nurse staffing quality data to the federal Hospital Compare website, and face civil money penalties for violations. The bill also protected nurses, hospital employees, and patients from retaliation for complaints about staffing.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients — who get more registered-nurse attention, fewer falls, infections, and medication errors — and registered nurses, who get safer workloads, a majority voice on staffing committees, the right to refuse unsafe assignments, and legal protection from retaliation for complaining about staffing. The bill's own findings cite research linking higher registered-nurse staffing to lower rates of falls, infections, medication errors, and death.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every Medicare-participating hospital to implement a hospital-wide nurse staffing plan setting an appropriate number of registered nurses for each unit and shift, aimed at safe, quality care.

Creates a nurse staffing committee in each hospital where at least 55 percent of members must be direct-care registered nurses, not managers or administrators, giving frontline nurses formal power over staffing decisions.

Allows a nurse to refuse an assignment that violates the staffing plan or that the nurse is not trained for, and protects nurses, hospital employees, and patients from retaliation for complaining or cooperating with investigations, with court remedies including reinstatement, lost wages, and damages.
Requires hospitals to post daily staffing numbers publicly and report them to HHS for publication on the Hospital Compare website, so patients can compare hospitals before choosing care.
Provides civil monetary penalties and enforcement through the Department of Health and Human Services for hospitals that violate the staffing requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have had to hire and schedule more registered nurses, run staffing committees, post and report staffing data, and risk civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with higher penalties for a pattern of violations. Those costs could be passed on through hospital prices or absorbed as lower margins.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise hospital labor costs by requiring more registered nurses on each unit and shift, and hospitals — including financially struggling rural and safety-net facilities — would bear that expense, which could pressure budgets for other services.
The bill did not set fixed nurse-to-patient ratios; it left minimum staffing levels to committees inside each hospital, which critics could argue lets hospitals write their own rules.
Civil money penalties for violations start at no more than $10,000 per knowing violation, a small sum for large hospital systems, unless the Secretary finds a pattern of violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — safer hospital care and less nurse burnout — was backed by research cited in the bill itself, including findings that inadequate staffing contributed to 24 percent of unanticipated patient-death or injury events [S3]. The main costs fall on hospitals: more nurse hours, committee overhead, public disclosure of staffing, and penalties. The bill's design was flexible rather than rigid — it did not mandate fixed nurse-to-patient ratios, instead letting unit-specific committees set minimums, and it exempted emergencies and gave rural hospitals four years to comply [S3]. An honest objection is that committee-driven plans can be slow and that compliance costs for hospitals might pressure other budgets; the counterargument from the bill's findings is that understaffing already carries large costs in errors, deaths, and nurse turnover exceeding a nurse's annual salary [S3]. The bill was never seriously tested, so the merits were never debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Daniel Inouye introduced the Registered Nurse Safe Staffing Act of 2010 in the Senate on June 15, 2010.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the bill had zero cosponsors.
After introduction, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call ever took place.
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and was never reintroduced in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The hospital industry is better off, because it never had to fund higher nurse staffing levels, public staffing disclosure, or enforcement penalties.

for.name: Sen. Daniel K. Inouye
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 15, 2010; it was his sole Senate action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 15, 2010 and took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.role: Hospitals that would bear the cost of mandated staffing
against.what_they_did: No lobbying campaign on this specific bill appears in the congressional record; noted only because hospitals were the bill's principal regulated party and it died without a hearing. Included under the widely-reported exception is the general fact that hospital associations historically opposed mandated nurse staffing ratios.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a party split because it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; a Democratic senator introduced it and no other senator, in either party, cosponsored it.

industries.note: Every Medicare-participating hospital would have to staff more registered nurses per unit and shift, stand up nurse-majority staffing committees, post daily staffing numbers, report quality data, and face civil penalties for violations. Staffing is a hospital's largest cost, so the bill would have cut into operating margins, particularly at facilities already running lean.

The bill gave frontline nurses a majority seat on staffing committees, the right to refuse unsafe assignments, and whistleblower protections against retaliation. The bill's own findings note that nearly 25 percent of nurses were considering leaving direct patient care because of inadequate staffing.

industries.industry: Nurse staffing agencies and temporary personnel firms
industries.note: Hospitals needing to raise staffing levels might hire more temporary and agency nurses to comply, though the bill requires reporting on the use of temporary agency personnel, which could also expose hospitals' reliance on them.
